blocks.text: An abstraction is a bet on the future. You are guessing which axis the product will vary along, and you are paying for that guess in every file that touches it. Boundaries are cheaper. A boundary says what may depend on what, and it keeps saying it long after the bet inside has lost.

In practice this means deciding ownership before deciding structure. If a route owns its state, then unmounting the route destroys the state and its subscriptions. That single rule removes an entire category of bug: the component that keeps updating after the user has navigated away, the service that accumulates listeners, the request that resolves into a destroyed view.

items: A feature may depend on core and shared. It may never depend on another feature.
Feature state is provided at the route, so disposal is automatic.
Cross-cutting services know about the domain. Features know about the screen.
The rule is enforced by an import lint check, not by review.

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you cannot delete a route in one commit without touching another feature, the boundary is in the wrong place.
Decide who owns the state, then how to store it

The storage question comes second, and it is much easier once ownership is settled. View state is synchronous, local and disposable — signals are the right shape for it. Server state is shared, concurrent and replayed — it wants a normalised store fed by intents, because two clients will change it at the same time and you need a rule for what happens then. URL state is shareable and restorable, so it belongs to the router.

The test for ownership is one sentence: if unmounting the route should destroy it, it is feature state; if two clients can change it at once, it belongs in the store. Everything else is a variation on those two cases, and the variations are where most of the confusion lives.
An architecture that ages well is one where the expensive decisions are still visible to the people who have to live with them.
Make the wrong thing harder than the right thing

Conventions decay. Lint rules, type constraints and generated documentation do not. If the correct behaviour is the path of least resistance, you get it for free; if it requires remembering, you get it for a quarter and then it is gone.

items: Required props are required at the type level, not in a doc comment.
Import direction is a lint error, not a code-review opinion.
Documentation is generated from the same declarations the build consumes.
Budgets are configuration read by CI and by the UI, so they cannot disagree.

blocks.text: None of this is glamorous. It is also the reason a three-year-old codebase can still be read in an afternoon, which is the only durability metric that has ever mattered to me.
